q-29179:
Recall that $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

First, we find the principal value:

$$
x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})={60}^{∘}
$$

Note that $x={60}^{∘}$ is not in the domain $-{360}^{∘}\le x<{0}^{∘}.$ To get a solution within the required domain, we subtract ${360}^{∘}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={60}^{∘}-{360}^{∘}=-{300}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={60}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the fouth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={60}^{∘}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13977622/assets/9c8adbb0a1594ae5bacfab7f1f92993c67659839599e10ab46d5cf98896e3ec7.png)

A second solution $X$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, and we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}X & ={360}^{∘}-{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={360}^{∘}-{60}^{∘} \\  & ={300}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $X={300}^{∘}$ is not in the domain $-{360}^{∘}\le x<{0}^{∘}.$ To get a solution within the required domain, we subtract ${360}^{∘}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} & ={300}^{∘}-{360}^{∘}=-{60}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-{60}^{∘},-{300}^{∘}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=-60\cdot (-300)=18\,000
$$

q-76503:
Recall that the range of $\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘}$ is given by

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

So, the equation $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=k$ has no solutions for $k\in (-1,1).$ 

Therefore, of the given equations, only equation I has no solutions.

q-29163:
Recall that the range of $\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ for $0\le x<2\pi $ is given by

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

So, the equation $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=k$ has no solutions for $k\in (-1,1).$ 

Therefore, of the given equations, only equation III has no solutions.

q-28519:
We're given that the quadratic equation has real coefficients and that $x=\frac{-2+7\text{i}}{2}=-1+\frac{7}{2}\text{i}$ is a root. Therefore, its complex conjugate $x=-1-\frac{7}{2}\text{i}=\frac{-2-7\text{i}}{2}$ is also a root.

q-28523:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and  $x=2\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate  $x=-2\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-2\text{i})(x+2\text{i})=0
$$

Multiplying out the parentheses and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4(-1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+4 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\pm 2\text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $3.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $3.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3({x}^{2}+4) & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}+12 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-28215:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=-1+\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate $x=-1-\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(-1+\text{i}))(x-(-1-\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(-1+\text{i})-x(-1-\text{i})+(-1+\text{i})(-1-\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+x-x\text{i}+x+x\text{i}+1-{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x+1+1 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x+2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-16935:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate $x=\frac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}\text{i}))(x-(\frac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(\frac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}\text{i})-x(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}\text{i})+(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}\text{i})(\frac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{x}{2}+x\sqrt{3}\text{i}-\frac{x}{2}-x\sqrt{3}\text{i}+\frac{1}{4}-3{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}+3 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-x+\frac{13}{4} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\frac{1}{2}\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $4.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $4.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4({x}^{2}-x+\frac{13}{4}) & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}-4x+13 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-32705:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(-\frac{2}{{y}^{2}}+2{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(-2{y}^{-2}+2{y}^{2}) \\  & =-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{-2})+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) \\  & =4{y}^{-3}+4y \\  & =\frac{4}{{y}^{3}}+4y \\  & =\frac{4+4{y}^{4}}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=\frac{{y}^{3}}{4+4{y}^{4}}.
$$

q-170140:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y-2{y}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y)-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}) \\  & =1-6{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1-6{y}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, substituting the point $(1,-1),$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(1,-1)} & =\frac{1}{1-6(-1)^{2}}=-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-32595:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(2\sqrt{y}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{y}}) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{y})-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{1/2})-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{-1/2}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}-3\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-3/2}) \\  & ={y}^{-1/2}+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{-3/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}+\frac{3}{2\sqrt{{y}^{3}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}+\frac{3}{2y\sqrt{y}} \\  & =\frac{2y+3}{2y\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=\frac{2y\sqrt{y}}{2y+3}.
$$

Finally, substituting the point $(5,9),$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(5,9)} & =\frac{2(9)\sqrt{9}}{2(9)+3}=\frac{18}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-32596:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3{y}^{2}-2y \\  & =2{y}^{2}-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2{y}^{2}-2y}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(9,3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(9,3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2(3)^{2}-2(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =\frac{1}{12}(x-9) \\ y & =\frac{x}{12}-\frac{3}{4}+3 \\ y & =\frac{x}{12}+\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-110192:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(5{y}^{3}-8{y}^{2}+16) \\  & =5\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3})-8\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})+16\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(1) \\  & =5\cdot (3{y}^{2})-8\cdot (2y)+0 \\  & =15{y}^{2}-16y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{15{y}^{2}-16y}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(24,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(24,2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{15\cdot {2}^{2}-16\cdot 2} \\  & =\frac{1}{28}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-2 & =\frac{1}{28}(x-24) \\ y & =\frac{x}{28}-\frac{6}{7}+2 \\ y & =\frac{x}{28}+\frac{8}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-1783:
The formula for ${}_{n}{P}_{r}$ is given by

$$
{}_{n}{P}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\,.
$$

$P(15,4)$ means the same thing as ${}_{15}{P}_{4}.$ Using the usual formula for ${}_{n}{P}_{r},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(15,4) & =\frac{15!}{(15-4)!} \\  & =\frac{15!}{11!} \\  & =\frac{15\cdot 14\cdot 13\cdot 12\cdot \cancel{11!}}{\cancel{11!}} \\  & =15\cdot 14\cdot 13\cdot 12 \\  & =32\,760.\end{aligned}
$$

q-122228:
The number of permutations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{P}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}.
$$

There are $9$ employees to choose from, so $n=9.$ We want to select $3$ of them for the three different shifts, so we have $r=3.$ 

Therefore, the number of different choices is

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{9}{P}_{3} & =\frac{9!}{(9-3)!} \\  & =\frac{9!}{6!} \\  & =\frac{9\cdot 8\cdot 7\cdot \cancel{6!}}{\cancel{6!}} \\  & =9\cdot 8\cdot 7 \\  & =504.\end{aligned}
$$

q-72824:
First, we find the principal value:

$$
x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-8)=-1.446\,4…≈-1.446\,4.
$$

Since $-1.446\,4$ lies outside the given domain, it is not a solution.

To generate more solutions, we add integer multiples of $\pi .$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\pi -1.446\,4≈1.695\,2, \\ {x}_{2} & =2\pi -1.446\,4≈4.836\,8.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}≈1.695\,2\cdot 4.836\,8≈8.2
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

q-120828:
First, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{2}{3})=41.810{…}^{∘}≈{41.81}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${41.81}^{∘}$ lies inside the range, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={41.81}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={41.81}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the second quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={41.81}^{∘}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13977985/assets/bc0c031fe6ccbb40dc77474582b301456f537ee2a649ba2d5b3bca9b1240618f.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $2$nd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={180}^{∘}-{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{41.81}^{∘} \\  & ={138.19}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions (rounded to the nearest integer) are $x={42}^{∘},{138}^{∘}.$
